title: The global spread of misinformation on spiders
screen_reason: Correspondence piece reporting an expert-coded content analysis of 5,348 online newspaper articles on spider-human encounters and bites from 81 countries and 40 languages, published 2010-2020. It states a share of items containing factual errors ('47% of articles containing errors'), verified by arachnologist experts, which is a CONTENT prevalence estimate with a stated denominator. The companion sensationalism share is recorded as QUALITY. Not a detection, intervention or belief study.

estimates.platform: online newspaper articles (regional, national and international press, traditional, online-only and magazine outlets)
estimates.measure_type: % of online newspaper articles about spider-human encounters and bites that contained factual errors, as judged by spider experts
estimates.value_raw: 47% of articles contained errors (no raw count printed; corpus n = 5,348 news items)
estimates.denominator: 5,348 online newspaper news items on spider-human interactions from 81 countries and 40 languages, published 2010-2020 (an expert-curated global database; 2,644 distinct spider-related events)
estimates.definition: An article was counted if expert reviewers identified factual error(s) in it - for spiders, typically misidentification of the species involved or incorrect information about bites and their danger
estimates.misinfo_def: The paper does not give a formal definition; it operationalises misinformation as poor information quality, i.e. "how information quality (sensationalism and errors) ... affect the global flow of information", within a study of "the global spread of (mis-)information on spiders"

estimates.page_loc: Opening summary, p. R871; restated in the Results narrative, p. R872 ('poor, with 47% of articles containing / errors and 43% being scored as sensationalistic by spider experts')
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Articles were scored by the paper's own network of spider experts (arachnologists among the 60+ co-authors), country by country and language by language; the text states sensationalism was 'scored as sensationalistic by spider experts' and that error and sensationalism coding procedures are in the Supplemental information and in the companion data paper (Mammola et al. 2022, Sci Data 9:109), neither of which is included in this text file. estimates.moderator_quote: For our analysis, we compiled 5,348 news items from 81 countries and 40 languages (Figure 1A). First, we asked: 'What is the quality of spider-related information in the global press and which news-level factors are associated with sensationalistic contents?'
estimates.notes: Single-issue topical news corpus (spider-human encounters and bites), so denom_scope=topical and denom_selection is left empty - the corpus is not rank-truncated, not a single source, and not multi-issue. The percentage is stated verbatim twice but no numerator count is printed, and the error-coding protocol lives in the Supplemental information / companion data paper, which the blindness rule prevented me from consulting; hence confidence medium. Pooled over an 11-year publication window (2010-2020) with no year-by-year breakdown in the text, so this is already a single collapsed point; year is set to the end of the collection window and the span is given in date. Note the internal count mismatch to flag: the text says 81 countries and Figure 1A says n = 79 pies plus 2,644 events - the 79 excludes Botswana and Iceland, for which no news was found. QUOTE NOTE: source_quote is taken from the opening summary because the Results-section sentence is broken by interleaved columns in this rendering; its contiguous fragments are 'poor, with 47% of articles containing' and 'errors and 43% being scored as'.

estimates.platform: online newspaper articles (regional, national and international press)
estimates.measure_type: % of online newspaper articles about spider-human encounters and bites scored as sensationalistic by spider experts
estimates.value_raw: 43% being scored as sensationalistic by spider experts (no raw count printed; corpus n = 5,348 news items)
estimates.denominator: 5,348 online newspaper news items on spider-human interactions from 81 countries and 40 languages, published 2010-2020
estimates.definition: An article was scored sensationalistic by expert reviewers on the basis of tone and framing (emotive, alarmist presentation of spider encounters), independently of whether its factual content was correct
estimates.misinfo_def: The paper does not give a formal definition; it operationalises misinformation as poor information quality, i.e. "how information quality (sensationalism and errors) ... affect the global flow of information"
estimates.page_loc: Opening summary, p. R871; restated in the Results narrative, p. R872 ('43% being scored as sensationalistic by spider experts')
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Scored by the paper's network of spider experts; protocol in the Supplemental information and companion data paper (not in this text file). No reliability statistic in the main text. Sensationalism and errors covary strongly in the paper's own regression ('there was a strong covariation between sensationalism and the presence of errors'; Errors [Present] odds-ratio SE 0.51 in Figure 1B).
estimates.moderator_quote: we used logistic regression to test for relationships between sensationalism and eight predictors at the news-article level
estimates.notes: Coded QUALITY rather than CONTENT because sensationalism is a judgement about tone: a wholly factually correct article can be scored sensationalistic, which is the paper's own position (it treats errors and sensationalism as two separate quality dimensions and models one as a predictor of the other). borderline=true because the paper's title and framing present sensationalism as part of 'misinformation on spiders'. Excluded from prevalence. QUOTE NOTE: the Results-section wording ('43% being scored as sensationalistic by spider experts') is split across interleaved columns in this rendering, so the source_quote is the opening summary's contiguous statement of the same figure.

missed_or_uncertain: Not extracted, with reasons: (a) '33% of all possible connections among countries are realized' - network density of the country-to-country news-flow graph; it is not a top-X-to-Y-of-activity statement, so it fails R1 and is not CONCENTRATION. (b) The regression and ERGM results (conditional R2 = 0.525, 45% of variance attributable to country/language/species, ~47% unexplained; all Figure 1B and 1C coefficients such as Errors [Present] and the effect of consulting a spider expert) - associations and model fit, not prevalence shares. (c) '~$78 billion annually' economic loss from fake news - a figure the paper cites from CHEQ/University of Baltimore (ref 8), excluded per R8. (d) No raw numerator counts are printed anywhere in the main text for either the error or sensationalism share, and no country-level or year-level breakdown is given numerically (country-level proportions appear only as pie-chart colours in Figure 1A), so no sub-rows are possible without inventing them. (e) The error-coding rubric itself (what counted as an error, who coded what, agreement) is in Supplemental information and the companion Sci Data paper, which the blindness rule kept me from opening - an adjudicator with access should verify the coder unit (article vs event) and whether the 47% is over articles or over the 2,644 events.

rob.design: Retrospective content analysis of an expert-curated global database of online newspaper articles on spider-human encounters and bites, 2010-2020: 5,348 news items covering 2,644 events across 81 countries and 40 languages, assembled and coded by a 60+ author network of arachnologists and collaborators (companion data paper: Mammola et al. 2022, Sci Data 9:109). Articles were scored by spider experts for factual errors and for sensationalism; article-level Bernoulli GLMM for sensationalism with eight news-level predictors controlling for species, language and country, plus an exponential random graph model of country-to-country news flow. No inter-rater reliability statistic, no numerator counts and no search protocol are reported in the main text; the outlet sampling frame per country is not described here, so coverage completeness cannot be assessed from this document.
